paper_title: FastOPD: On-Policy Distillation for Lightweight VLA Deployment

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models have scaled rapidly to enhance manipulation performance and generalizability, but this scaling incurs high computational costs that render real-world deployment increasingly challenging. Existing approaches typically mitigate this issue by designing smaller architectures or reducing the iterative denoising steps in flow-based policies. In this work, we propose FastOPD, a foundation-to-lightweight VLA framework that enables the practical deployment of large-scale VLAs through efficient on-policy distillation. Specifically, FastOPD adapts a flow map for single-state teacher supervision and combines it with a self-consistency objective to construct a compact student that learns the teacher dynamics. Furthermore, we theoretically demonstrate that minimizing this objective allows the distilled student to recover a distribution on par with that induced by an ideal few-step teacher model. We evaluate FastOPD across diverse foundation policies in simulation and real-world experiments. On LIBERO, FastOPD retains 84% of the performance of $π_{0.5}$ with only two inference steps, reducing inference latency by 78.1% while outperforming existing few-step distillation baselines in average success rate. With LingBot-VLA as the teacher, FastOPD improves the single-step success rate over the base student by 15.9 percentage points on RoboTwin 2.0. We further demonstrate its applicability to a World Action Model (WAM) and deploy a compact student distilled from MolmoAct2 on a real robot.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Recent progress in robot learning has moved toward large-scale foundation policies, ranging from Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (Collaboration, 2024; Black et al., 2025b;a; Bjorck et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026a) to emerging World Action Models (WAMs) (Kim et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026). In particular, recent methods such as DreamZero (Ye et al., 2026) and Cosmos Policy (Kim et al., 2026) leverage pretrained video generation models *Equal contribution. Blue arrows denote student transitions; red arrows denote teacher velocities. to capture rich visual dynamics and achieve strong generalization and manipulation performance. However, these powerful foundation priors also lead to increasingly large policy backbones and high computational cost, creating tension between model capability and deployment efficiency on physical robots. Lightweight VLA models such as SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025) address the efficiency side of this trade-off by directly designing smaller policies with less than 0.5B parameters. complementary direction is to transfer the capability of powerful foundation policy into compact student through knowledge distillation. Knowledge Distillation (KD) (Hinton et al., 2015; Mansourian et al., 2025) has been widely studied for transferring the capability of large teacher model into smaller student. Specifically, On-Policy Distillation (OPD) (Agarwal et al., 2024) supervises the student using teacher predictions on its own generated trajectories, reducing distribution mismatch and compounding errors from offline distillation. OPD also provides dense supervision along the student trajectory, in contrast to the sparse rewards commonly used in reinforcement learning. While OPD has been actively explored in LLM post-training, recent works have extended it to diffusion and flow models (Li et al., 2026a; Fang et al., 2026b). However, directly applying OPD to flow-based policies is computationally inefficient. It requires rolling out the students denoising trajectory and repeatedly evaluating the teacher at the visited timesteps, resulting in high training cost for large foundation teachers. In this work, we revisit few-step flow-map models through the lens of on-policy distillation (OPD) and introduce FastOPD, foundation-to-lightweight VLA framework for efficient policy distillation. Our goal is to transfer the capabilities of large-scale VLA into compact student while substantially reducing both training and inference costs, without sacrificing policy performance (see Fig. 1). To reduce the training cost of conventional OPD, FastOPD combines on-policy teacher supervision of the students velocity field with self-consistency objective (Frans et al., 2025). Rather than querying teacher supervision throughout an entire generation trajectory, the self-consistency objective propagates local velocity supervision to finite-interval shortcut transitions, as illustrated in Fig. 2. This allows the student to approximate the teacher dynamics without explicitly constructing or evaluating teacher flow map over each shortcut transition. We further show theoretically that FastOPD implicitly recovers the distribution induced by the teachers ideal shortcut model, providing distributional justification for few-step distillation. Importantly, the same self-consistency formulation naturally induces an any-step flow map (Boffi et al., 2024; Song et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Geng et al., 2025; Sabour et al., 2025), allowing the distilled student to operate with substantially fewer sampling steps at inference. FastOPD therefore compresses the foundation VLA along two complementary dimensions: model capacity and sampling complexity, enabling deployment on resource-constrained, consumer-grade hardware. The proposed formulation also enables stable training in the challenging few-step regime without adversarial objectives or costly higher-order derivative computations. concurrent work, VLAOPD (Zhong et al., 2026), also studies on-policy distillation for VLA models, but primarily uses expert supervision to improve policy performance. In contrast, FastOPD focuses on transferring foundation policy into lightweight few-step student. We evaluate FastOPD on two simulation benchmarks and one real-world manipulation task, using diverse foundation teachers with 3B6B parameters (Black et al., 2025a; Yuan et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026a). To maximize both architectural and inference efficiency, we adopt SmolVLA as 2 Preprint. the lightweight student policy. We compare against representative few-step distillation methods, including CTM, DMD, and iMF. Across these settings, FastOPD enables the compact student to recover up to 84% of the performance of teacher models that are more than 7.3 larger, using only one or two sampling steps. This substantially reduces inference cost while retaining large fraction of the foundation policys performance. To the best of our knowledge, FastOPD is the first OPD framework for VLAs that jointly reduces both model size and the number of sampling steps while retaining the capabilities of large-scale foundation policy.

While these models capture high-quality multimodal action distributions, accurate integration typically requires many denoising steps, motivating few-step distillation for faster inference. Vision-Language-Action Models. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (Collaboration, 2024; Black et al., 2025b;a; Bjorck et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2024; Octo Model Team et al., 2024) couple pretrained vision-language backbone with an action decoding head to map an observation and language instruction to distribution over robot actions, most commonly via flow or diffusion action expert (Chi et al., 2023; Black et al., 2025b) trained with flow matching loss. Recent foundation VLA models illustrate the scale required for strong multi-task generalization, typically exceeding 2B parameters and trained on over 10,000 hours of multimodal robot data spanning multiple embodiments (Black et al., 2025b;a; Wu et al., 2026), but remain expensive to deploy. Several works (Octo Model Team et al., 2024; Shukor et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2025; Reuss et al., 2025) instead train smaller VLAs; SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025), for example, reduces model size to 450 million parameters by using small VLM and layer skipping. However, it still requires =10 denoising steps per action chunk and does not benefit from the capabilities of larger foundation policies. Flow Map Models. wide range of few-step generative methods aim to reduce iterative sampling cost. Distillation-based approaches (Sabour et al., 2025; Boffi et al., 2024), including Consistency Models (CM) (Song et al., 2023), and Consistency Trajectory Models (CTM) (Kim et al., 2024), distill pre-trained multi-step teacher into few-step student, while score-distillation methods directly match teacher and student distributions (Yin et al., 2024b;a). sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Our experiments span two multitask simulation benchmarks (Sec. 4.1) and one real-robot task (Sec. 4.2). We freeze the visionlanguage backbone and fine-tune only the action expert and projections with the additional time projection layer described in Sec. 3. We evaluate each method using 1, 2, 4, and 10 denoising steps and compare it against the teacher and the initial student with 50 trials per task. Full experimental details are provided in Appendix B. 4.1 SIMULATION EXPERIMENTS Benchmarks. We evaluate FastOPD on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) and RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025). LIBERO evaluates single-arm manipulation across four standard evaluation suitesSpatial, Object, Goal, and Longcomprising 40 tasks in total. RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025) comprises 50 challenging bimanual manipulation tasks, with 2,500 demonstrations collected in clean scenes and 25,000 demonstrations collected under heavy scene randomization. We report results in both clean and randomized settings on unseen environments. Baselines. For simulation experiments, we compare our method with three representative approaches to few-step generation: Consistency Trajectory Model (CTM) (Kim et al., 2024), Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) (Yin et al., 2024b;a), and improved Mean Flow (iMF) (Geng et al., 2026). Since iMF was originally formulated for training from scratch, we adapt it to the distillation setting by replacing its self-referential instantaneous velocity target with the teacher velocity. Notably, our method consistently achieves performance gains in the few-step regime, improving the single-step success rate of the base student from 35.3% to 51.2%, and outperforms all few-step distillation baselines at every sampling step. It does so at latency comparable to SmolVLA, while being 10.0 faster than the LingBot-VLA teacher. At 4 and 10 steps, FastOPD performs slightly below the base student, indicating that its benefit lies mainly in the few-step regime where the base student degrades. Distilling World Action Model. Recent World Action Models (WAMs) build on pretrained video generation models and have emerged as an alternative to foundation VLAs (Kim et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026). To examine whether FastOPD extends beyond VLA teachers, we distill Fast-WAM (Yuan et al., 2026), 6B-parameter video-based teacher, into the same 451M SmolVLA student with an identical training recipe. As shown in Tab. 2, the student distilled from Fast-WAM achieves 50.5% average success rate at single denoising step, 15.2 percentage points over the initial SmolVLA baseline (35.3%). Furthermore, it reaches 56.3% at two steps, successfully transferring knowledge despite the substantial differences in architecture and pretraining between the teacher and the student. This demonstrates that FastOPD is versatile approach that applies not only to VLAs but also to WAMs, since it only requires the teachers velocity field on the students own action trajectories, regardless of how the teacher is built. 4.2 REAL-WORLD EXPERIMENTS To validate its real-world applicability, we further design real-world robot scenario, pnp-plate, in which the robot picks up the ball and places it on the plate. Experiments use the right arm of bimanual YAM robot with parallel-jaw gripper and top-view and wrist-mounted cameras that provide RGB observations. We train MolmoAct2 (Fang et al., 2026a), an action reasoning model that is suitable for real-world deployment, on our collected demonstrations for 14,000 iterations and use the resulting policy as the teacher. We initialize the student from SmolVLA, warm it up on the collected demonstrations with the standard flow matching objective (i.e., behavior cloning) for 10,000 iterations, and subsequently distill the teacher into the student using FastOPD. Full experimental details are provided in Appendix B.5. Figure 5: Real-world results on the pnp-plate task. (a) Success rate (%). (b) Task completion time (s), averaged over successful episodes. Figure 6: FastOPD on pnp-plate: (a) start, (b) transport, and (c) placement. Each panel shows the top view with the wrist view inset (lower left). Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 summarize the results. With four denoising steps, FastOPD achieves 50% success rate, improving by 8 percentage points over the 42% of the base SmolVLA at the same number of steps. Notably, FastOPD shows faster and more accurate performance than the 10-step base student, improving the success rate from 44% to 50% while cutting the execution time from 19.32 to 17.38 s. These results demonstrate that FastOPD can transfer the capability of larger teacher to compact student deployed on physical robot with few steps. 4.3 ABLATION STUDY Training efficiency. FastOPD reduces training overhead by supervising the student at single sampled on-policy state rather than across all denoising steps. As illustrated in Fig. 1, standard OPD (Li et al., 2026a) takes 9.51 hours per 1,000 training iterations while FastOPD requires only 1.43 hours, achieving 5.7 speedup. This translates directly into accelerated convergence  (Fig. 1)  . FastOPD achieves 78.2% 1-step success rate in just 10 hours, whereas conventional OPD requires Preprint. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this paper, we present FastOPD, an efficient on-policy distillation framework that transfers largescale VLAs into lightweight student models to maximize computational efficiency without compromising performance. Specifically, FastOPD streamlines the iterative denoising process by anchoring single on-policy state to the teacher, coupled with self-consistency objective for finiteinterval transitions. In simulation and real-robot experiments across diverse VLA and WAM teachers, FastOPD improves over the base student in the few-step regime and outperforms existing fewstep distillation methods, while substantially reducing training and inference cost. We hope this framework facilitates scalable, real-time deployment of foundation policies on physical robots. 9 Preprint.
